coredata.dc:description: Due to its toxic effects in aquatic organisms and in humans, Bisphenol A (BPA) has been replaced by Bisphenol S (BPS) as additive in the production of epoxy glues, baby bottles, cardboard, thermal paper, among others. In this study, the removal of chronic toxicity of BPS from aqueous solution was evaluated by adsorption on powdered activated carbon (PAC) using commercial carbons from two distinct matrices (vegetal and mineral). The characterization of adsorbents was performed by infrared spectroscopy, surface area BET (Brunauer, Eminett e Teller), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and zeta potential. The adsorption kinetics and isotherms were evaluated. The chronic toxicity was measured through assays with the organism Ceriodaphnia dubia for 7 days. The kinetics for both absorbents were fitted to pseudo-second-order models in experimental initial conditions of 2 mg L−1 and 30 mg L−1, pH 6.5 and temperature of 25 °C, with removal efficiency of 94 % at equilibrium in 60 min for mineral PAC and of 88 % in 120 min for vegetal PAC. Furthermore, the isotherm model proposed by Freundlich presented the best settings for both PAC. Activated carbon adsorption may be an efficient method for the reduction of chronic toxicity, reaching no observed effect concentration (NOEC) in the organisms at 1.56 μg BPS L−1.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Due to its toxic effects in aquatic organisms and in humans, Bisphenol A (BPA) has been replaced by Bisphenol S (BPS) as additive in the production of epoxy glues, baby bottles, cardboard, thermal paper, among others. In this study, the removal of chronic toxicity of BPS from aqueous solution was evaluated by adsorption on powdered activated carbon (PAC) using commercial carbons from two distinct matrices (vegetal and mineral). The characterization of adsorbents was performed by infrared spectroscopy, surface area BET (Brunauer, Eminett e Teller), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and zeta potential. The adsorption kinetics and isotherms were evaluated. The chronic toxicity was measured through assays with the organism Ceriodaphnia dubia for 7 days. The kinetics for both absorbents were fitted to pseudo-second-order models in experimental initial conditions of 2 mg L−1 and 30 mg L−1, pH 6.5 and temperature of 25 °C, with removal efficiency of 94 % at equilibrium in 60 min for mineral PAC and of 88 % in 120 min for vegetal PAC. Furthermore, the isotherm model proposed by Freundlich presented the best settings for both PAC. Activated carbon adsorption may be an efficient method for the reduction of chronic toxicity, reaching no observed effect concentration (NOEC) in the organisms at 1.56 μg BPS L−1.

ce:section.ce:para: The development of technologies is increasing quickly worldwide, and the use of plastics is increasing concomitantly. Nonetheless, most cities have not invested in appropriate systems to manage all their plastic waste. In 2016, the world managed 242 million tons of plastic waste, which correspond to 12 % of all solid waste [1]. All this progress causes the increase of solid waste pollution, causing degradation of the environment both in soil and in aquatic ecosystems. Bisphenol A (BPA) or 2.2-bis [4-hydroxyfenil] propane is a monomer used as industrial additive to produce polycarbonate plastics, epoxy resins, phenolic resins, can coating, toys, eyeglass lenses, electronics, and other industrial products [2–4]. Many studies point out that the exposure to BPA can cause endocrine disruption and/ or be toxic to organisms, causing disorders in their metabolic and reproductive systems [5–7].

Due to the restriction of BPA application since it can be harmful for both the environment and for human health, it was developed an alternative monomer known as Bisphenol S (BPS) (4.4′- sulfonyldiphenol) [8]. The BPS is applied in the production of epoxy glues, baby bottles, pet food cans, notepaper, cardboard and thermal paper. Due to its similar structure to BPA (Fig. 1 ), studies were developed to measure its toxicity. Many toxic effects of BPA in aquatic species in different trophic levels are known, but BPS has few detailed studies with experiments in vivo in aquatic ecotoxicology [9].

In samples of sludge from wastewater treatment plants located in South Korea and the United States, concentrations of 44.9 ng BPS g−1 and 34.5 ng BPS g−1, respectively, were reported [10–12]. In humans, this pollutant was found in urine in a concentration range of 0.02–21.0 ng mL−1 [13,14]. The concentrations of BPS detected in samples of water and urine are at the same order of magnitude than BPA [15].

The replacement of BPA for BPS has been occurring on a large scale [16–18]. Therefore, the evaluation of BPS toxicity shows relevance to avoid the same problems caused by BPA (impacts on the environment and human health).

Some studies present the toxic effects of BPS, e.g., Zhao et al. [15] evaluated its genotoxic potential in male zebrafish (Danio rerio) at concentrations of 1–100.0 μg L−1 for 28 days. The results of this study showed that the exposure to BPS affects glucose homeostasis of the fish, possibly by hampering the physiological effect of insulin, and higher BPS doses pronouncedly interfered with glucose metabolism. Also, BPS acute toxicity in Swiss albino mice after the weaning phase was assessed by exposing them for 10 weeks to concentrations of 25, 50 and 100 μg kg−1 day−1 [17]. This exposure generated physiological disturbances and toxicological effects, such as alteration in orexigenic hypothalamic neuropeptide (AgRP), causing appetite disorders that have resulted in increased food intake and body weight gain [17]. Wei et al. [12] demonstrated that the long term exposure of zebrafish to water containing 1.0–100.0 μg L−1 can cause thyroid disorders in the exposed organisms and in their descendants, modifying the plasmatic levels of thyroid hormone (TH), the genes linked to the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis and the histology of the thyroid follicle. Nevertheless, studies concerning the ecotoxic effects of BPS are necessary to understand their extension in different trophic levels. These studies may help to design wastewater treatment processes that properly degrade or remove BPS from sewages and industrial effluents to avoid its discharge in the environment, reducing the toxic effects of this compound.

Thoene et al. [19] reviewed pathophysiological articles that show a strong correlation between the exposure to BPS and the incidence of cancer, metabolic disorders, obesity, DNA damage, liver damage, neural damage, oxidative stress and, most often, endocrine and reproductive effects, considering many different types of tissues and cell cultures from mice to humans, for in vitro studies, and zebrafish as animal model, for in vivo studies.

Some treatment processes for the removal of BPS in aqueous solutions are reported in the literature, such as activated sludge process [20], advanced oxidation oxidative processes [21–23] and adsorption on carbonaceous materials [24,25].

The use of more sustainable and environmentally friendly processes for water and wastewater treatment is recommended. Additionally, sustainable conversion of organic waste into useful products is becoming increasingly important for the environment and carbon-rich waste can be effectively used to produce activated carbon [26]. Therefore, the use of activated carbon as part of a wastewater treatment process is sustainable, can be regenerated after saturation of its active sites and, compared to other purification methods, is low-cost [27,28]. The adsorption on activated carbon is commonly used to remove micropollutants and substances that persist after biological treatment [29]. Synthetic wastewater containing 5 mg of each bisphenol (BPA, BPF, BPS, and 4-tert-BP) per liter was treated at two laboratory-scale vertical-flow constructed wetlands (CWs) for 8 weeks [24]. Besides the common reed (Phragmites australis), one of the CW mediums included pumice rock (normal CW) and the other, pumice rock with activated carbon (AC-CW). The activated carbon (AC) as a wetland medium improved the removal efficiency of contaminants (78 % BPS removal for normal CW and 100 % for AC-CW) and provided microbial growth (one-two orders higher than CW) that may have contributed to BPS degradation [24].

The objective of this study was to evaluate the removal of chronic toxicity of BPS from aqueous solution through adsorption on powdered activated carbon. For this purpose, chronic toxicity was assessed with microcrustacean Ceriodaphnia dubia. The adsorbents used in this study have been characterized for the best elucidation of the phenomena that occurred between BPS and their surface. The solution used as effluent in this study simulates the concentration of bisphenol-S commonly observed in sanitary and industrial wastewaters to be discharged in water bodies.

ce:section.ce:section-title: BPS stock solution and quantification methodology
ce:section.ce:para: The BPS was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, purity > 99 %. A stock solution of 100 mg L−1 was prepared by dilution in deionized water. This solution was prepared on a magnetic stirrer plate for 24 h, until the complete dissolution of BPS. The deionized water was obtained through the purification system of Gehaka. The quantification of BPS was carried out using a spectrophotometer Shimadzu UV-1800 at 197 nm (wavelength that presented the higher absorbance for BPS solution). A standard curve was constructed for a range of 0.12–2.0 mg L−1 [30,31].

Two types of powdered activated carbon were used: PAC C (Carbomafra C-117), an activated carbon of vegetal origin (coconut shell) purchased from Indústrias Químicas Carbomafra (Curitiba, Brazil) and PAC S (Norit SAE Super), an activated carbon of mineral origin (bituminous), purchased from Cabot do Brasil (São Paulo, Brazil).

The functional groups present on the surface of both powdered activated carbon were analyzed in an infrared spectroscopy Fourier transform, model Nicolet 6700IR, performed in a spectral range from 400 to 4000 cm−1 and with a resolution of 4 cm-1. PAC samples were mixtured with KBr to produce a tablet to be analyzed. The Surface Area BET [32] method was used to characterize the surface area of the absorbents of this study in equipment ASAP 2000, Micrometrics. The superficial area BET is an analysis which provides the adsorption area, volume, and pore size of carbon, through curves of adsorption-desorption of N2 (gaseous).

The texture characterization and the assessment of mineral impurities in both PAC were performed by Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), TM1000 Tabletop Microscope. Zeta potentials were measured at different pH levels on the equipment Malvern Zetasizer coupled to a Malvern multi-purpose titrator (MPT-2).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Experiments for equilibrium time and adsorption kinetics determination
ce:section.ce:para: The aqueous solution of BPS (2 mg L−1) was prepared from the stock solution (100 mg L−1) diluted in deionized water. The concentration of BPS in the feed solution of this study (2 mg L−1) was selected to fit the detection capacity of the UV–vis spectrophotometer method. The experiments of both PAC were carried out with 100 mL of feed solution and 30 mg L−1 in Erlenmeyer flasks using a stirring table at a constant temperature of 25 °C and rotation speed of 240 rpm. Samples were taken every 15 min in the first hour and every 30 min until 3 h of stirring. The samples were filtered in 0.45 μm membrane and analyzed by UV spectrophotometry. Blank experiments with BPS feed solution in the same conditions described above but without PAC were performed.

To evaluate the results, two kinetics models were used: the pseudo-first-order model (Langergren equation), which is presented in Eq. (1) [33] and in its integrated form in Eq. (2); and the pseudo-second-order model, which is presented in Eq. (3) [34] and in its integrated form in Eq. (4).
(1) dq/dt = k1 (qe-qt)
(2) log (qe-qt) = log qe – k1×t/2.303
where k1 (min−1) is rate constant for a kinetic of the pseudo-first order; qe (μg mg−1) is the quantity of adsorbate that was adsorbed at equilibrium; qt is the quantity adsorbed at time t and t (min) is the adsorption time.
(3) dqt/dt = k2 (qe – qt)2
(4) 1/qt = 1/ (k2×qe 2) + t/qe
where k2 (μg g−1 min−1) is the rate constant for a kinetic model of pseudo-second order.

For adsorption isotherm determination, the experimental conditions were: initial concentration of 2 mg L−1, sample pH of 6.5, temperature of 25 °C and volume of 100 mL. The concentrations of the PAC C and S varied in the range of 20–60 mg L−1. The samples were filtered and analyzed in the same way as in item 2.4. After the experiments, the adsorption capacity (q, μg mg−1) was calculated according to Eq. (5) [35]:
(5) q = (Co – Ce) / (m × V)
where Co (μg L−1) is the initial concentration of BPS, Ce (μg L−1) is the concentration of BPS at equilibrium, V (L) is the experiment volume and m (mg) is the mass of adsorbent material. Models of isotherms applied were Langmuir and Freundlich [36]. Langmuir and Freundlich isotherm models are the two most used when adsorption on activated carbon studies are performed for the removal of contaminants in water or effluents as a treatment step [36]. The mathematical isotherm models of Langmuir and Freundlich are presented in Eqs. (6) and (7) [37,38].
(6) qe = qmax × b × Ce / (1 + b × Ce)
where qmax is an empiric constant that indicates the adsorption capacity in a monolayer (μg mg−1) of Langmuir isotherm and b is a constant associated with the free adsorption energy.
(7) qe = Kf × Ce 1/n
where Kf is an experimental constant that is related to the adsorption capacity of BPS onto PAC and 1/n is a constant that represents the adsorption strength.

This study simulates the presence of bisphenol-S in effluents to be discharged in water bodies. In this case, the environmental laws of some states of Brazil use microcrustaceans as an indicator of toxicity in treated effluents. Among them, Ceriodaphnia dubia is more sensitive to compounds commonly present in effluent samples when compared to other microcrustaceans, such as Daphnia magna [39].

Ceriodaphnia dubia is from the order Cladocera, family Daphniidae and it is a zooplankton microcrustacean. It was selected as a standard test-organism in the chronic toxicity assay of this study due to the following advantages: life cycle relatively short (between 30 and 40 days); possibility to be cultivated in laboratory since the adult individuals present length of 0.8 – 0.9 mm; reproduction in normal conditions by parthenogenesis (first brood varies from 3 to 5 days) with genetically identical descendants, ensuring uniformity of answers in the assays; and sensitivity to the majority of substances potentially toxic in low concentrations [40]. In addition, C. dubia plays a major role in the food chain in freshwater environments. Considered as primary consumer (filter feeders), they feed on algae and serve as food to secondary consumers, as fishes and other vertebrates. Therefore, changes in behavior and the survival of C. dubia can interfere directly in other trophic levels of the aquatic ecosystem [41,42].

For the chronic toxicity assays, the BPS solution was prepared by dilution in methanol and later in deionized water (final methanol concentration < 0,01 %). The chronic toxicity assays with microcrustaceans C. dubia were performed according to ABNT (Brazilian Association of Technical Standards) and ISO (Internacional Organization for Standardization) [41,43]. Reproduction rate was used as the endpoint for determining chronic toxicity after 168 h (7 days) of exposure to Bisphenol S in 7 serial dilutions of factor 2 (100 μg L−1 in 100 %, 50 %, 25 %, 125%, 6.25 %, 3.12 % and 1.56 %) (n = 10). The negative control (blank, n = 10) and solvent control (methanol at the highest solvent concentration of 0.01 %, n = 10) were also performed. In each beaker of 20 mL, 15 mL of sample (test solution) or culture solution (negative control) and a female between 6 and 24 h old were added. The assay was conducted in a cycle of light/dark of 16 h/8 h inside an incubator with a cold light at 25 °C and organisms were fed every two days with algal cultures. The vials were cleaned, and the neonates were counted daily. At the end of 168 h, a comparison was carried out between the average number of neonates produced (chronic toxicity) and survivor females in the correspondent flasks for each concentration. These numbers were also compared with the negative and the solvent control groups.

The validity of the tests was confirmed according to the criterion in ABNT and ISO standards [41,43]. Significant effects between each BPS concentration and the controls (negative and solvent) on the reproduction rate of exposed C. dubia were evaluated by analyses of variance one-way ANOVA (p < 0.05), followed by Dunnett’s post hoc tests using the software GraphPad Prism 5 (v. 5.02 for Windows, San Diego, USA).
Fig. 2 illustrates the infrared spectra of both activated carbons evaluated.

Functional groups on activated carbon surfaces can be the result of the carbonaceous origin and the activation method that carbon went through (physical or chemical). It is possible to note, in both FTIR spectra, a large band in the region of 3400−3500 cm−1, which stands for a stretch OH bond of phenolic groups or carboxylic acid [44]. Bands in the range of 1570−1580 cm−1 and 1100 cm−1 are characteristic of CC bond of aromatic compounds and the vibration of CO bond of ethers or alcohols, respectively [45]. These bands are also identified in both spectra of FTIR activated carbons. Bands that appear only for mineral origin carbon (PAC S, Fig. 2b) in the region of 1460 and 875 cm−1 demonstrate the presence of methylene groups and the distortion of CH bond out of the plane, respectively. Nonetheless, for PAC C, Fig. 2a presents a band in the region of 1634 cm−1, which is assigned to vibrations of CO of carboxylates, resulting oxidation of aromatic rings of benzene in the lignin, that also indicates the presence of acids, anhydrides and lactones, very common in PAC from vegetal origin [46,47].

Table 1 shows the results of characterization of the superficial area and porosity of adsorbents used in this study. The micropore area, external area and micropore volume for PAC S are 22 %, 29 % and 23 % greater than the ones for PAC C, respectively. According to Weber [48], the lower the size of particles and the greater the porosity of a solid adsorbent, the greater its specific surface area and, consequently, the greater will be its adsorption capacity.
The results of PAC S BET superficial area are in accordance with previous results for different PAC [36] that obtained the range of 950−1050 m2 g−1 for mineral origin activated carbons.

Fig. 3 shows the adsorption-desorption isotherms. According to the classification of isotherms BET [32], PAC C presents a type II isotherm, which indicates the presence of pores whose size is greater than the average volume of molecules adsorbed during BET isotherm experiments (N2). In these systems, there is a predominance of physical and continuous adsorption, with a progressive increase of adsorbed layers, which is known as multilayer adsorption.

PAC S presents the behavior of type I isotherm. In general, the physical adsorption is established, therefore, PAC S behavior indicates the predominance of micropores, and the adsorption takes place only inside of them [49].

In SEM analysis, PAC S showed a black, intense color, particles finely separated, round flakes and uniformity in its structure (Fig. 4 a and b). This structural specification can be related to the origin of precursor organic material (bituminous). For PAC C, the material did not present uniformity in the distribution and size of particles (Fig. 4c and d). The particles of PAC C, differently from the ones of PAC S, presented the form of blades, which can be related to the fact of the carbon be produced from the vegetal precursor material, more specifically, coconut shell.

The zeta potential analysis is important for characterizing the electro-kinetics behavior of PAC. The pH value at the point in which zeta potential equals zero is called the isoelectric point (IEP) of the interface [50]. The isoelectric point depends on the nature of the solid and on the composition of the aqueous solution [51]. Fig. 5 presents the variation of the adsorbents’ surface charge over the pH of the solution.

PAC C has two isoelectric points, at pH 7.11 and 10.2. Below 7.11 and above 10.2, PAC C presents negative surface charges and, in the pH range between IEP, the surface presents positive charges. On the other hand, PAC S presents positive surface charges at pH < 2.72, which is its only isoelectric point. Thus, PAC S presents negative surface charge at pH values above 2.72.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Experiments of equilibrium time and adsorption kinetics determination
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 6 illustrates the results obtained in the experiments carried out with both PAC in contact with BPS solution.

The equilibrium was established at 60 min of adsorption for PAC S, reaching 94 % removal of BPS. For PAC C, the adsorption equilibrium was established around 120 min, with 88 % removal of BPS. The adsorption capacity of BPS, for both PAC, is higher in the beginning, since there is a larger available superficial area for adsorption. As process progresses, the number of available pores is reduced and the BPS molecules already adsorbed start to repel the ones still in the solution, which makes the adsorption of new molecules reduce in longer contact periods [52]. The results demonstrated that the adsorption of BPS on PAC C (vegetal origin) was less efficient than the one on PAC S (mineral origin). The adsorption capacities of both PAC were 56.4 μg BPS mg−1 for PAC S and 52.2 μg BPS mg−1 for PAC C. Even though the average pore sizes of both carbons are similar, PAC C presents characteristics of low-porosity carbon and, thus, the adsorption of BPS is hampered by BPS molecule size.
Fig. 7 presents the fitting of the observed results to the kinetics models (pseudo-first-order model and pseudo-second-order model). Table 2 resumes the kinetics parameters for both PAC used.

The correlation coefficient (R2) indicates that the adsorption of BPS on both adsorbents is better described by the pseudo-second-order model. Even though the R2 values were higher than 0.9 for both adsorbents using the pseudo-first-order model (PAC C = 0.97 and PAC S = 0.91), the values of predicted qe obtained from the fitting to pseudo-second-order model are much closer to the experimental qe observed. Consequently, the results suggest that the chemisorption (covalent bond forces and exchange of electrons between adsorbent and adsorbates) may be the rate-limiting step of adsorption kinetics [29,53,54].

López-Ramos et al. [55] evaluated the adsorption of BPA and BPS solutions (201 mg L−1 and 220.3 mg L−1, respectively) on chemically modified activated carbons (dosage of 0.1 – 0.4 g L−1) and the results were also better adjusted to pseudo-second-order model. Sui and Chai [56] evaluated the adsorption of three bromophenols (BP) in aqueous solution (100–1000 mg L – 1) using hazelnut shell activated carbon (dosage of 4 g L−1). The equilibrium was reached in 5 min and the adsorption of all BP studied were better adjusted to pseudo-second-order model, as well. Kinetics evaluation of Bisphenol-AF (BPAF) removal from aqueous solutions (5–200 mg L −1) using synthesized activated carbonalginate beads (0.05 g L−1) also showed better fitting to pseudo-second-order model [57]. All these results show that, regardless of the adsorbent used, the adsorption kinetics of bisphenol (regardless of its many different substituents) in aqueous solution is better represented by the pseudo-second-order model.

There are few data about BPS adsorption capacities in published literature. The values observed in the present study were close to the ones reported by Li et al. [25], which were 61.5 μg BPS per mg of activated carbon. Other adsorbent materials were evaluated, such as nanozeolite NaY assisted by quaternary ammonium salt (25.64 μg BPS per mg of nanozeolite [58]) and reduced graphene oxide (261.74 μg BPS per mg of graphene [25]).

Fig. 8 presents the values of qe as a function of concentration of BPS at equilibrium (Ce) for both PAC and their isotherms of Freundlich and Langmuir. The removal efficiencies of BPS in the experiment with PAC S reached 89.8–99.2% and PAC C, 86.2–96.1% (BPS initial concentration of 2 mg L−1 and PAC dosage of 20–60 mg L−1).

Langmuir isotherm model did not represent the real behavior of adsorption results because it is based on adsorption happening only at specific and homogeneous sites on the adsorbent surface [59] and probably the surfaces of PAC used in this study present heterogeneous sites. In general, Freundlich model fits better the results of industrial effluent adsorption and the ones of adsorbents that have heterogeneous surfaces [36]. The experimental results of BPS adsorption were better fitted to the Freundlich isotherm for both activated carbons studied.

Table 3 presents the parameters obtained from the Freundlich isotherm. The parameter Kf indicates the activated carbon adsorptive capacity and an n value between 2 and 10 indicates favorable adsorption of BPS on PAC in the Freundlich isotherm model [60]. The results show the PAC S presented adsorptive capacity almost 3.3 times greater than PAC C. This result is corroborated by the characterization of PAC and by the source matrix.

Koduro et al. [61] evaluated the adsorption of bisphenol A (1–60 μg BPA L−1) onto goethite iron oxide particles impregnated with activated carbon composite (dosage of 170 mg L−1). The authors concluded the Freundlich isotherm model was considered more suitable than the Langmuir isotherm for the adsorption of BPA. Machado et al. [62] investigated the adsorption of bisphenol A in a solution (20 mg L−1) on granular activated carbon from mineral matrix (dosage of 0.5 g L−1) and the results were better fitted to Freundlich isotherm, as well (R2 = 0.99).

The adsorption phenomena between PAC and BPS can be explained by the electrophoretic mobility of PAC C and S and the protonation balance of BPS. The surfaces of the CAP are negatively charged in pH > 2.72 (PAC S) and pH < 7.11 (PAC C) and BPS solution in this study presents pH = 6.5. The pKa of BPS is 8.2 and it is mainly in its neutral form at pH < 7.0 [26]. Deprotonated BPS species (BPSH−, BPS2-) are found in BPS solutions with pH values in the range of 7–11 [55] and, consequently, during adsorption, there is repulsion between the negatively charged surface of PAC C or PAC S and the anionic species of BPS [26,55,58].

The pH of a solution directly influences the adsorption mechanism [59], since, at very acid pH, there can be competition between H+ ions and adsorbate for the adsorption sites on the carbon. In addition, when species are ionized, they present greater water affinity, thus reducing their adsorption on activated carbon. On the other hand, at high pH values, competition with OH− ions can also occur [59]. Therefore, when the pH is in a range where the molecules are in their neutral form, the adsorption capacity is relatively higher.

Li et al. [25] performed BPS adsorption tests on reduced graphene oxide (rGo) and verified the influence of pH on adsorption efficiency. The authors concluded that the best pH range for the adsorption of BPS is between 6.0 and 7.0, where the neutral form of BPS is predominant.

The results of zeta potential for the adsorbents revealed that both PAC mostly present negative surface charge. FTIR analyses confirmed the presence of oxygenated functional groups and corroborated the zeta potential data. However, PAC C presents a less intense negative charge density because of the presence of CO group. Since BPS is a compound with high electron density, it could be easily repelled by the surface of both PAC. Therefore, considering that the solution pH is 6.5, BPS could be slightly protonated, resulting in a higher density of positive charge in its structure and a greater adsorption on PAC S.
Fig. 9 presents results of the chronic toxicity assays with C. dubia, showing concentrations of BPS versus the number of neonates of test-organism.

The assays demonstrated satisfactory sensitivity and the results show that the lowest observed effect concentration (LOEC) was 3.12 μg BPS L−1 and the no observed effect concentration (NOEC) was 1.56 μg BPS L−1.

Park et al. [9] evaluated acute toxicity of BPS (0.5–100 mg L−1), using the aquatic organism Brachionus koreanus (planktonic rotifers). The authors obtained a LC50 % greater than 100 mg L−1. In their case, the observed effect may be some enzymatic oxidative stress. Liu et al. [63] evaluated acute toxicity during 48 h to BPS different concentrations (100, 75, 50, 25 and 12.5 mg L−1) using Daphnia magna (planktonic crustacean). They observed immobilization of daphnids after 48 h of acute exposure and EC50 was 6.2 mg L−1. The authors concluded that D. magna does not present sensibility for BPS and considered the aquatic organism C. dubia more suitable for evaluating the effects of BPS. Also, according to Guo et al. [64] in the case of bisphenol A, the exposure of invertebrate and fish species reproductive endpoints is generally more sensitive than non-reproductive ones.

The results of the chronic toxicity assay in this study has demonstrated to be appropriate for the evaluation of BPS toxic effect at very low concentrations. Therefore, this implies that BPS, one of BPA substitutes, also causes toxic effects on the environment and may not be adequate for that purpose.

The results obtained in this study for BPS adsorption on PAC were better fitted to the isotherm model proposed by Freundlich. The mathematical expressions for both PAC are shown in Eqs. (8) and (9) for PAC C and PAC S, respectively:
(8) qe = . 3.13 Ce 0.5228 (for Carbon C)
(9) qe = . 10.5 Ce 0.3955 (for Carbon S)

Therefore, considering the Eqs. (8) and (9), for the total removal of chronic toxicity in solutions with an initial concentration of 2 mg L−1, which means reaching the NOEC (Ce = 1.56 μg BPS L−1), the PAC C dosage would be 535.5 mg L −1 and the PAC S dosage would be 159.6 mg L−1. Since PAC S has a larger surface area, less impurities and better adsorption results, its necessary dosage for the proper removal of chronic toxicity is around three times lower than the one of PAC C. According to Eckenfelder [36], these toxicity-reducing PAC S concentrations are acceptable for full-scale treatment. Thus, PAC adsorption for BPS removal in water or wastewater can be economically viable, especially if the exhausted PAC is reused after regeneration or reactivation [29].

This study investigated the adsorption on powdered activated carbon for the removal of bisphenol S from aqueous matrices. After the characterization of the two distinct evaluated PAC, PAC S, from mineral origin, presented larger superficial BET area (958.16 m2 g−1) compared to the PAC C, from vegetal origin (726.68 m2 g−1). The adsorption kinetics was evaluated, and the pseudo-second-order model best represented the experimental adsorption data for both PAC. Freundlich isotherm properly described the adsorption of BPS on both activated carbons. PAC S presented higher BPS removal percentage, reaching values of 99.2 % after 2 h of experiment. The chronic ecotoxicity assay with microcrustacean C. dubia was sensitive to BPS toxicity and it presented NOEC of 1.56 μg BPS L−1. Therefore, the use of the activated carbons evaluated in this study (dosages of 535.5 mg PAC C L-1 and 159.6 mg PAC S L−1 for a solution with initial concentration of 2 mg L−1) makes it possible to reach a concentration of BPS that do not cause toxicity (C. dubia) to aquatic environments.
